claim: Arabidopsis thaliana is a vascular plant that serves as a central genetic model and universal reference organism in plant and crop science.
source: The vascular plant Arabidopsis thaliana is a central genetic model and universal reference organism in plant and crop science.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of A. thaliana's role in science.

claim: A. thaliana supports the most advanced systems biology approaches among all land plants.
source: The availability and active development of experimental tools and resources, in combination with the accessibility of a wealth of cumulatively acquired knowledge about this plant, support the most advanced systems biology approaches among all land plants.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and represents an assertion about A. thaliana's capabilities relative to other land plants.

claim: A. thaliana is a small, annual or winter annual, rosette plant.
source: Arabidopsis thaliana is a small, annual or winter annual, rosette plant (Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1 showing the plant morphology.

claim: A. thaliana belongs to the taxonomic family Brassicaceae in the eudicotyledonous group of angiosperm vascular plants.
source: It belongs to the taxonomic family of the Brassicaceae in the eudicotyledonous group of angiosperm vascular plants (see Box 1 for a glossary of specialist terms used in this article).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the taxonomic classification of A. thaliana.

claim: The Brassicaceae family includes rapeseed, brussel sprouts, various cabbages, cauliflower, garden radish and mustard.
source: This family also includes morphologically diverse but closely related oilseed crops, vegetables and spice plants, for example rapeseed, brussel sprouts, various cabbages, cauliflower, garden radish and mustard.
evidence: This is directly stated as examples of plants in the Brassicaceae family.

claim: A. thaliana was first described by Johannes Thal in the Harz Mountains of Northern Germany in 1577.
source: First described by the physician Johannes Thal in the Harz Mountains of Northern Germany in 1577, A. thaliana featured in the Species Plantarum II published by Linnaeus in 1753, and it received its present name, Arabidopsis thaliana (L.) Heynh, from Gustav Heynhold in 1842 (Kück, 2005).
evidence: This historical fact is stated with a citation to Kück, 2005.

claim: A. thaliana featured in the Species Plantarum II published by Linnaeus in 1753.
source: First described by the physician Johannes Thal in the Harz Mountains of Northern Germany in 1577, A. thaliana featured in the Species Plantarum II published by Linnaeus in 1753, and it received its present name, Arabidopsis thaliana (L.) Heynh, from Gustav Heynhold in 1842 (Kück, 2005).
evidence: This historical fact is stated with a citation to Kück, 2005.

claim: A. thaliana received its present name from Gustav Heynhold in 1842.
source: First described by the physician Johannes Thal in the Harz Mountains of Northern Germany in 1577, A. thaliana featured in the Species Plantarum II published by Linnaeus in 1753, and it received its present name, Arabidopsis thaliana (L.) Heynh, from Gustav Heynhold in 1842 (Kück, 2005).
evidence: This historical fact is stated with a citation to Kück, 2005.

claim: Friedrich Laibach published an influential cytogenetic study on A. thaliana in 1907.
source: Friedrich Laibach was the first researcher to publish an influential cytogenetic study on A. thaliana in 1907, to foster genetics in the 1940s, and to systematically collect accessions in the wild after emphasizing the extent of intraspecific phenotypic variation in A. thaliana in the 1950s (Somerville and Koornneef, 2002; Koornneef and Meinke, 2010).
evidence: This historical fact is stated with citations to Somerville and Koornneef, 2002 and Koornneef and Meinke, 2010.

claim: Friedrich Laibach systematically collected A. thaliana accessions in the wild after emphasizing the extent of intraspecific phenotypic variation in the 1950s.
source: Friedrich Laibach was the first researcher to publish an influential cytogenetic study on A. thaliana in 1907, to foster genetics in the 1940s, and to systematically collect accessions in the wild after emphasizing the extent of intraspecific phenotypic variation in A. thaliana in the 1950s (Somerville and Koornneef, 2002; Koornneef and Meinke, 2010).
evidence: This historical fact is stated with citations to Somerville and Koornneef, 2002 and Koornneef and Meinke, 2010.

claim: The popularity of A. thaliana as a model organism took off in the 1980s.
source: The popularity of A. thaliana as a model organism took off in the 1980s, and then rapidly gained momentum when researchers successfully began to combine genetics with powerful molecular biology methods.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the historical timeline of A. thaliana's adoption as a model organism.

claim: The Arabidopsis reference genome sequence was published as the first nuclear genome of a flowering plant in 2000.
source: The Arabidopsis reference genome sequence was published as the first nuclear genome of a flowering plant in 2000 (http://www.arabidopsis.org/) (Arabidopsis Genome Initiative, 2000; Somerville and Koornneef, 2002; Koornneef and Meinke, 2010).
evidence: This is stated directly with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: A. thaliana has allowed fundamental progress in knowledge of molecular principles of plant development, cell biology, metabolism, physiology, genetics and epigenetics.
source: The ease and speed with which experiments can be conducted on A. thaliana has allowed enormous fundamental progress in our knowledge of the molecular principles of plant development, cell biology, metabolism, physiology, genetics and epigenetics (http://www.arabidopsisbook.org/).
evidence: This is directly stated as an outcome of using A. thaliana as a model organism.

claim: The sister group of A. thaliana includes Arabidopsis lyrata, Arabidopsis arenosa, Arabidopsis croatica, Arabidopsis halleri, Arabidopsis cebennensis and Arabidopsis pedemontana.
source: Indeed, the natural history of A. thaliana differs notably from that of the species in its sister group of the most closely related existing plant species, which includes Arabidopsis lyrata, Arabidopsis arenosa and Arabidopsis croatica, and the three species Arabidopsis halleri, Arabidopsis cebennensis and Arabidopsis pedemontana (Koch and Matschinger, 2007; Hohmann et al., 2014) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations and supported by Figure 2.

claim: The divergence time of the common ancestor of A. thaliana and its sister species was estimated at around 5 million years ago.
source: The divergence time of the common ancestor of these species and the A. thaliana lineage was estimated at around 5 million years ago (Mya) (Koch et al., 2000), with upper and lower bounds of 17.9 and 3.1 Mya (Koch et al., 2000; Beilstein et al., 2010; Ossowski et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations providing the estimate and bounds.

claim: Divergence of A. thaliana from its sister species occurred immediately before or during the transition from a warm period to progressively colder climates.
source: Thus, divergence occurred immediately before or during the transition from a warm period to progressively colder climates, followed by rapid glacial cycles from 3 Mya until the latest glacial maximum about 18,000 years ago.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the divergence time estimate.

claim: There was a natural allopolyploidization event between A. arenosa and A. thaliana 10,000–300,000 years ago, giving rise to Arabidopsis suecica.
source: There has even been a natural allopolyploidization event between A. arenosa and A. thaliana 10,000–300,000 years ago, giving rise to Arabidopsis suecica (Sall et al., 2003; Jakobsson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations supporting the claim.

claim: A. thaliana is recognized as native to Western Eurasia.
source: Arabidopsis thaliana is recognized as native to Western Eurasia (Figure 3).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by Figure 3 showing the distribution.

claim: A. thaliana is a colonizer and pioneer plant of disturbed, poor, stony or shallow soils.
source: The species is a colonizer and pioneer plant of disturbed, poor, stony or shallow soils, and it can also be found in nutrient-poor, often sandy, meadow and forest habitats (Mitchell-Olds and Schmitt, 2006).
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation.

claim: Sequence polymorphism data provide evidence for a historical expansion of the A. thaliana species population.
source: Sequence polymorphism data provide evidence for a historical expansion of the A. thaliana species population (Nordborg et al., 2005; Schmid et al., 2005), thus differing from the known demographic histories of the non-hybrid species in its sister group in the Arabidopsis genus (Wright et al., 2003; Heidel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations to studies providing the sequence polymorphism data.

claim: A. thaliana re-colonized Central Europe from glacial refugia in the Caucasus or Balkans between ∼10,000 and 5000 years ago, possibly accompanying the spread of human farming from the Near East.
source: It has been suggested that A. thaliana re-colonized Central Europe from glacial refugia in the Caucasus or Balkans between ∼10,000 and 5000 years ago, possibly accompanying the spread of human farming from the Near East (Francois et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion with a citation.

claim: There is evidence for additional glacial refugia for A. thaliana in the Mediterranean region, including the North African Atlas Mountains.
source: There is also clear evidence for additional glacial refugia for A. thaliana in the Mediterranean region, including the North African Atlas Mountains (Brennan et al., 2014), and for additional migration (for example, from the Iberian peninsula in a northeastern direction [Sharbel et al., 2000; Pico et al., 2008]), as well as for population structure reflecting isolation by distance in Eurasia (Nordborg et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citations providing evidence.

claim: In the past few 100 years, A. thaliana has expanded its geographic and climatic range in synanthropy, migrating to and across North America, southward in Africa, and more recently to East Asia.
source: In the past few 100 years, A. thaliana has further expanded its geographic and climatic range in synanthropy (see Glossary), migrating to and across North America, as well as southward in Africa, and more recently to East Asia (see Figure 3).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by Figure 3.

claim: The present climatic and geographic range of A. thaliana is larger than that of any of its close relatives.
source: The present climatic and geographic range of A. thaliana is larger than that of any of its close relatives, which have either not expanded into warmer climates or are local endemics (Koch and Matschinger, 2007; Hohmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: A. thaliana has undergone transitions to reproduction by self-fertilization (selfing).
source: In addition to—and likely permitting—the rapid expansion of its range, A. thaliana has undergone transitions to reproduction by self-fertilization (selfing).
evidence: This is directly stated as a characteristic of A. thaliana.

claim: Transitions to selfing in A. thaliana occurred at around 0.4 Mya or around ≥1 Mya based on different approaches.
source: Estimates place these transitions as having occurred, based on different approaches, at around 0.4 Mya or around ≥1 Mya (Bechsgaard et al., 2006; Tang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to studies providing the estimates.

claim: Most species closely related to A. thaliana are either predominantly or strictly outcrossing.
source: By contrast, most species closely related to A. thaliana are either predominantly or strictly outcrossing (the latter if species are strongly self-incompatible).
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to A. thaliana's selfing behavior.

claim: A. thaliana is an annual plant with a rapid life cycle that can be as short as 6–8 weeks in some accessions.
source: In addition to selfing, A. thaliana is an annual plant with a rapid life cycle that can be as short as 6–8 weeks in some accessions, whereas most of its close relatives are biannuals or herbaceous perennials (Al-Shehbaz and O'Kane, 2002) (see Figures 1, 2).
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation and supported by Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Most close relatives of A. thaliana are biannuals or herbaceous perennials.
source: In addition to selfing, A. thaliana is an annual plant with a rapid life cycle that can be as short as 6–8 weeks in some accessions, whereas most of its close relatives are biannuals or herbaceous perennials (Al-Shehbaz and O'Kane, 2002) (see Figures 1, 2).
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation and supported by Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Vegetative A. thaliana plants are smaller in size than most of its close relatives.
source: Vegetative A. thaliana plants are smaller in size than most of its close relatives, and their survival and reproduction are comparably robust in a variety of environments.
evidence: This is directly stated as a comparison.

claim: The leaves of A. thaliana are positioned to form a more compact rosette than in A. halleri.
source: The leaves of A. thaliana are positioned to form a more compact rosette, and inflorescences are more erect and elongated, than in its close relative A. halleri.
evidence: This is directly stated as a morphological comparison.

claim: The flowering of A. thaliana is highly synchronized compared to its sister group of species.
source: By comparison to its sister group of species, the flowering of A. thaliana is highly synchronized, with the formation of a larger number of siliques (seed pods) per plant, each containing a higher, or far higher, number of seeds that are smaller in size compared to those of its relatives.
evidence: This is directly stated as a comparison.

claim: A. thaliana forms a larger number of siliques per plant than its relatives.
source: By comparison to its sister group of species, the flowering of A. thaliana is highly synchronized, with the formation of a larger number of siliques (seed pods) per plant, each containing a higher, or far higher, number of seeds that are smaller in size compared to those of its relatives.
evidence: This is directly stated as a comparison.

claim: Seeds of A. thaliana are long-lived and highly viable by comparison to those of A. halleri and A. lyrata.
source: Seeds of A. thaliana are long-lived and highly viable by comparison to those of A. halleri and A. lyrata (Ute Krämer, personal observation).
evidence: This is stated based on personal observation.

claim: The roots of A. thaliana mostly contain only a single layer of each specialized cell type.
source: Notably, its roots mostly contain only a single layer of each specialized cell type, a feature that is optimal for in vivo imaging (Figure 4) (De Lucas and Brady, 2013).
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation and supported by Figure 4.

claim: The roots of A. halleri contain two additional cell layers compared to A. thaliana.
source: This organization differs from the roots of its close relative A. halleri, which contain two additional cell layers (Hanikenne et al., 2008), and is in stark contrast to root tissues composed of multiple cell layers, as found in many other plants.
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation.

claim: The ancestral number of chromosomes in the Brassicaceae (n = 8) is conserved in A. thaliana's closest relatives.
source: The ancestral number of chromosomes in the Brassicaceae (n = 8) is conserved in A. thaliana's closest relatives.
evidence: This is directly stated as a fact about chromosome numbers.

claim: The genome of diploid A. thaliana is rearranged, with two sets of n = 5 chromosomes.
source: By comparison, the genome of the diploid A. thaliana is rearranged, with two sets of n = 5 chromosomes.
evidence: This is directly stated as a characteristic of A. thaliana's genome.

claim: A. thaliana has a genome size of 157 Mbp, one of the smallest known genomes among flowering plants.
source: This is associated with a pronounced reduction in genome size in A. thaliana, down to 157 Mbp (Bennett et al., 2003) (reference genome assembly of 135 Mbp)—one of the smallest known genomes among flowering plants.
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation.

claim: The nuclear genome size of A. lyrata is 207 Mbp for the reference assembly.
source: For comparison, nuclear genome sizes of its closest relatives are larger, mostly due to a higher abundance of transposable elements in euchromatic regions, with 207 Mbp for the reference assembly of the nuclear genome of A. lyrata (Hu et al., 2011), and about 260 Mbp estimated for A. halleri (Johnston et al., 2005; Peer et al., 2006; Hohmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation.

claim: The nuclear genome size of A. halleri is estimated at about 260 Mbp.
source: For comparison, nuclear genome sizes of its closest relatives are larger, mostly due to a higher abundance of transposable elements in euchromatic regions, with 207 Mbp for the reference assembly of the nuclear genome of A. lyrata (Hu et al., 2011), and about 260 Mbp estimated for A. halleri (Johnston et al., 2005; Peer et al., 2006; Hohmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: The larger genome sizes of A. thaliana's closest relatives are mostly due to a higher abundance of transposable elements in euchromatic regions.
source: For comparison, nuclear genome sizes of its closest relatives are larger, mostly due to a higher abundance of transposable elements in euchromatic regions, with 207 Mbp for the reference assembly of the nuclear genome of A. lyrata (Hu et al., 2011), and about 260 Mbp estimated for A. halleri (Johnston et al., 2005; Peer et al., 2006; Hohmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: Classical molecular genetics approaches have been used in A. thaliana to dissect the patterning and development of flowers.
source: Classical molecular genetics approaches have been used in A. thaliana to dissect the patterning and development of flowers (Meyerowitz et al., 1991), embryos (Mayer et al., 1991), leaves and roots (Di Laurenzio et al., 1996), and of the maintenance of stem cell niches at the plant's growing tips.
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation.

claim: The biology of A. thaliana is rich in temperature- and light-dependent regulation.
source: The biology of A. thaliana is rich in temperature- and light-dependent regulation, some of which might be triggered by photosynthates (see Glossary) rather than by light itself (Haydon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation.

claim: Some temperature- and light-dependent regulation in A. thaliana might be triggered by photosynthates rather than by light itself.
source: The biology of A. thaliana is rich in temperature- and light-dependent regulation, some of which might be triggered by photosynthates (see Glossary) rather than by light itself (Haydon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility with a citation.

claim: Contemporary global warming appears to proceed faster than the local adaptation of A. thaliana populations.
source: Nevertheless, contemporary global warming appears to proceed faster than the local adaptation of A. thaliana populations (Wilczek et al., 2014), based on the reproductive fitness of plants grown at locations across the European distribution range from stored seeds, which were collected in different geographic regions between 4 and 70 years earlier.
evidence: This is stated with a citation and based on experimental data.

claim: Phenotypic plasticity and utilizing limited local resources in bare habitats for rapid and ample reproduction appear to be characteristics of the life history of A. thaliana.
source: Phenotypic plasticity and utilizing limited local resources in bare habitats for rapid and ample reproduction appear to be characteristics of the life history of A. thaliana.
evidence: This is directly stated as an interpretation of A. thaliana's life history.

claim: The roots of the Brassicaceae generally do not undergo mycorrhizal or rhizobial symbiosis.
source: In contrast to the vast majority of flowering plants, the roots of the Brassicaceae generally do not undergo mycorrhizal or rhizobial symbiosis.
evidence: This is directly stated as a characteristic of the Brassicaceae family.

claim: The absence of mycorrhizal or rhizobial symbiosis is likely to make A. thaliana comparably independent of specific soil microbes or microbiomes.
source: This is likely to make A. thaliana comparably independent of specific soil microbes or microbiomes, which may be advantageous for a colonizer of recently disturbed and exposed soils.
evidence: This is stated as a likely consequence with reasoning.

claim: The biosynthesis of nicotianamine through nicotianamine synthase was identified in A. thaliana before its discovery in other kingdoms of life.
source: Some of the central molecular components of these pathways have been identified in A. thaliana before their discovery in other kingdoms of life, for example, the biosynthesis of low-molecular-weight chelators for micronutrient metal cations through nicotianamine synthase (Trampczynska et al., 2006; Schuler et al., 2012), and for both micronutrient and non-essential toxic metal cations through phytochelatin synthase (Clemens, 2006; Tennstedt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: The biosynthesis of chelators through phytochelatin synthase was identified in A. thaliana before its discovery in other kingdoms of life.
source: Some of the central molecular components of these pathways have been identified in A. thaliana before their discovery in other kingdoms of life, for example, the biosynthesis of low-molecular-weight chelators for micronutrient metal cations through nicotianamine synthase (Trampczynska et al., 2006; Schuler et al., 2012), and for both micronutrient and non-essential toxic metal cations through phytochelatin synthase (Clemens, 2006; Tennstedt et al., 2009).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: Genetically controlled within-species variation is observed in leaf nutrient concentrations when natural accessions of A. thaliana are cultivated under uniform controlled conditions.
source: When natural accessions of A. thaliana are cultivated under uniform controlled conditions, genetically controlled within-species variation is observed in leaf nutrient concentrations (Atwell et al., 2010), which appears to be adaptive at least in some cases (Poormohammad Kiani et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: A. halleri is one of approximately 500 known metal hyperaccumulator plant species.
source: As one out of a total of ∼500 known metal hyperaccumulator plant species (see Glossary), A. halleri accumulates extraordinarily high concentrations of zinc and cadmium in leaves where these metals act as a so-called elemental defense against biotic stress (Boyd, 2010; Krämer, 2010).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: A. halleri accumulates extraordinarily high concentrations of zinc and cadmium in leaves where these metals act as an elemental defense against biotic stress.
source: As one out of a total of ∼500 known metal hyperaccumulator plant species (see Glossary), A. halleri accumulates extraordinarily high concentrations of zinc and cadmium in leaves where these metals act as a so-called elemental defense against biotic stress (Boyd, 2010; Krämer, 2010).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: Calamine soils rich in zinc, cadmium and lead are readily colonized by A. halleri.
source: Calamine soils rich in zinc, cadmium and lead—commonly as a result of anthropogenic pollution—are readily colonized by A. halleri (Ernst, 1974; Krämer, 2010), and occasionally by A. arenosa (Przedpełska and Wierzbicka, 2007).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: There are natural populations of A. arenosa and A. lyrata on nutrient-poor ultramafic soils.
source: In addition, there are some natural populations of A. arenosa and A. lyrata on nutrient-poor ultramafic soils (Holubover serpentinite, 2002; Turner et al., 2010), which contain high levels of nickel and magnesium originating from the local bedrock (see Glossary).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: Populations of A. lyrata characteristically inhabit calcareous outcrops.
source: Finally, populations of A. lyrata (Al-Shehbaz and O'Kane, 2002) and A. croatica (Plants, 2014) characteristically inhabit calcareous outcrops (see Glossary).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: Populations of A. croatica characteristically inhabit calcareous outcrops.
source: Finally, populations of A. lyrata (Al-Shehbaz and O'Kane, 2002) and A. croatica (Plants, 2014) characteristically inhabit calcareous outcrops (see Glossary).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: Microbial communities associated with A. thaliana appear to be more strongly influenced by soil type than by plant genotype.
source: Above-ground (Vorholt, 2012; Horton et al., 2014) and below-ground organs of A. thaliana, and their immediate vicinity, provide habitats for microbial communities, which appear to be more strongly influenced by soil type than by plant genotype (Bulgarelli et al., 2012; Lundberg et al., 2012; Schlaeppi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: Once A. thaliana has initiated reproductive development, reproduction is favored over defense.
source: Once A. thaliana has initiated reproductive development, reproduction is favored over defense (Winter et al., 2011).
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation.

claim: Similarities have been noted between plant defenses and animal innate immunity relating to the domain architectures of NLR protein receptors.
source: Similarities have been noted between plant defenses and animal innate immunity. These relate primarily to the domain architectures of NLR (nucleotide-binding domain leucine-rich repeat) protein receptors (see Glossary) that function in the detection of biotic attack, and the programmed cell death that occurs as a host defense response (Maekawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation.

claim: Arabidopsis possesses effective defenses against herbivory with an important role for secondary metabolites.
source: Arabidopsis possesses effective defenses against herbivory, for example by insects and snails, with an important role for secondary metabolites.
evidence: This is directly stated as a characteristic of Arabidopsis.

claim: Glucosinolates are converted to pungent and toxic breakdown products in damaged tissues.
source: Most prominently, a class of sulfur-rich compounds, called glucosinolates (see Glossary), are converted to pungent and toxic breakdown products in damaged tissues (Halkier and Gershenzon, 2006).
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation.

claim: Upon leaf wounding, the systemic activation of defenses in distant leaves involves the long-distance movement of electrical surface potential changes at velocities between 43 and 150 µm s−1 involving ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR)-related membrane proteins.
source: Upon leaf wounding, the systemic activation of defenses in distant leaves involves the long-distance movement of electrical surface potential changes at velocities between 43 and 150 µm s−1 involving ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR)-related membrane proteins (Mousavi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation.

claim: Upon exposure of A. thaliana to salt stress, a systemic signal moves from root to shoot in the form of a Ca2+ wave at a velocity of 400 µm s−1, requiring the vacuolar ion channel TPC1.
source: For example, upon exposure of A. thaliana to salt stress, a systemic signal moves from root to shoot in the form of a Ca2+ wave at a velocity of 400 µm s−1, requiring the vacuolar ion channel TPC1 (Two Pore Ca2+ Channel protein 1) (Choi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation.

claim: Plants of the Brassicaceae family were classified as calciotrophic, based on their ability to store comparably large quantities of dissolved calcium.
source: With respect to nutrient ions, plants of the Brassicaceae family were classified as calciotrophic, based on their ability to store comparably large quantities of dissolved calcium (Ca2+) (Kinzel, 1982).
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation.

claim: In calciotrophic plants, leaf Ca concentrations are generally higher than leaf potassium concentrations.
source: In calciotrophic plants, leaf Ca concentrations are generally higher than leaf potassium concentrations, as is common in the Brassicaceae, Papaveraceae and Resedaceae families, but rare in other plant families.
evidence: This is directly stated as a characteristic of calciotrophic plants.

claim: The large capacity that Brassicaceae family members have for storing divalent cations in their vacuoles might explain why this family comprises ∼50% of all known metal hyperaccumulator plant taxa.
source: The large capacity that Brassicaceae family members have for storing divalent cations in their vacuoles might explain why this family comprises ∼50% of all known metal hyperaccumulator plant taxa (Krämer, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation with a citation.

claim: The Brassicaceae family comprises approximately 50% of all known metal hyperaccumulator plant taxa.
source: The large capacity that Brassicaceae family members have for storing divalent cations in their vacuoles might explain why this family comprises ∼50% of all known metal hyperaccumulator plant taxa (Krämer, 2010).
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation.

claim: The absence of adaptation to extreme osmotic conditions in A. thaliana could result from its metabolism, which appears to generally avoid high internal osmotic potentials by storing osmotically inactive starch instead of osmotically active photosynthetic sugars.
source: Moreover, the absence of adaptation to extreme osmotic conditions in A. thaliana could result from its metabolism, which appears to generally avoid high internal osmotic potentials by storing osmotically inactive starch instead of osmotically active photosynthetic sugars (Streb and Zeeman, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation with a citation.

claim: The Brassicaceae exhibit an active sulfur metabolism and a comparably elevated requirement for sulfate as a nutrient in the soil.
source: Finally, in association with the high sulfur content of glucosinolates, the Brassicaceae exhibit an active sulfur metabolism and a comparably elevated requirement for sulfate as a nutrient in the soil (Marschner, 1995).
evidence: This is directly stated with a citation.

claim: Insights into the molecular functions of genes in A. thaliana have proven invaluable for identifying the genetic basis of agronomically important traits in crops, such as plant height and flowering time.
source: Insights into the molecular functions of a multitude of individual genes, as well as the elucidation of biosynthetic pathways and regulatory networks in A. thaliana, have proven invaluable for identifying the genetic basis of agronomically important traits in crops, such as plant height and flowering time (Doebley et al., 2006; Olsen and Wendel, 2013).
evidence: This is directly stated with citations.

claim: The successful transfer of complex molecular knowledge from A. thaliana to crops requires accounting for between-species differences in natural history.
source: The successful transfer of more complex molecular knowledge from A. thaliana to crops requires us to account for between-species differences in natural history.
evidence: This is directly stated as a requirement.

claim: The natural history of A. thaliana is likely to impose fundamental limitations on its validity as a model for investigating agronomically relevant traits related to the maintenance of growth and survival under stress.
source: However, the natural history of A. thaliana is likely to impose some fundamental limitations on its validity as a model for investigating agronomically relevant traits related to the maintenance of growth and survival under stress.
evidence: This is directly stated as a likely limitation.
